approach: Resolve the 10√2 N force into horizontal and vertical parts, find the normal reaction, compare the net horizontal force with the maximum static friction, then compute kinetic friction and acceleration.

steps.text: Resolve the 10√2 N force into horizontal and vertical components at 45°.
Find the normal reaction from the vertical balance: weight and the 6 N force act down, the vertical part of the 10√2 N force acts up.
Find the total applied horizontal force and compare it with the maximum static friction.
steps.equation: F = 4 + 10 = 14 N; f(max static) = μₛR = 0.6×16 = 9.6 N

steps.text: Since 14 N exceeds 9.6 N, the block moves, so kinetic friction acts instead.
Find the acceleration from the net horizontal force.

final_answer.value: (a) friction = 6.4 N, kinetic; (b) the block moves, with acceleration 3.8 m/s²

common_mistakes.text: Taking the normal reaction as only the weight, R = 20 N, instead of adjusting for the 6 N and 10 N vertical forces, gives friction = 8 N and a = 3 m/s².
Adding the 10 N vertical component instead of subtracting it gives R = 36 N and friction = 14.4 N, close to canceling the applied force entirely.
